content: Patients who remained at home until their death were studied in a systematic review conducted by Brainard et al. in 2016. This review aimed to analyze behaviors and quantify the odds of acquiring infections with the Ebola virus or Marburg virus. The findings highlighted that direct contact with a corpse, its body fluids, or contaminated items significantly increased the risk of transmission. Activities such as washing and dressing the body also posed a high risk. These results suggest that funeral attendance, particularly involving direct contact with the body or contaminated objects, contributes to the increased risk of transmission. Ebola virus and Marburg virus are introduced into human populations through zoonotic transmission. Human-to-human transmission occurs via direct or indirect contact with the blood or other body fluids of infected individuals. This transmission chain is typically more sustained with the Ebola virus than with the Marburg virus, indicating that the Marburg virus may be inherently less infectious. While all body fluids can carry the virus, blood and fluids contaminated with blood present the highest risk. Transmission can occur through direct or indirect contact, as well as splashes or sprays of infected fluids. Certain high-risk activities increase the likelihood of human-to-human transmission.g., eyes, mouth) or broken skin to the virus in the absence of appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), needlestick or sharps injuries with contaminated equipment, and close unprotected contact with individuals in the later stages of Ebola or Marburg disease. Preparing a recently deceased body for burial, such as washing or dressing it without PPE, also poses a risk, although evidence on this is inconsistent. Other modes of transmission include sexual transmission, mother-to-child transmission, and transmission during breastfeeding, though these are not the focus of this guideline. The communicability period for Ebola and Marburg viruses begins on the day symptoms appear. Neither virus is known to be transmissible before symptom onset. Viral shedding may persist in certain body fluids, such as semen and breast milk, even after the virus is no longer detectable in the blood. This must be considered when providing discharge instructions. Infection prevention and control (IPC) is critical in mitigating and containing the spread of Ebola and Marburg viruses. During outbreaks, IPC efforts should extend to all points of health-seeking behavior, including government and private facilities, traditional healers, and treatment centers. Strengthening IPC preparedness and operational readiness is essential to contain outbreaks and prevent healthcare systems from becoming overwhelmed. When an outbreak is imminent or ongoing, it is crucial to evaluate existing IPC capacity to identify gaps and prioritize interventions. Categorizing geographic zones and healthcare facilities by their emergency phase facilitates planning and resource allocation. The IPC ring approach, which provides rapid, intensive, and short-term IPC support to areas of active transmission, has been effective in breaking transmission chains and preventing healthcare-associated infections during past outbreaks. The IPC ring approach involves several key steps: decontaminating healthcare facilities, providing IPC kits, training healthcare workers, and engaging with communities to heighten awareness and distribute hygiene kits. This approach was successfully implemented during the West African Ebola outbreak (2014–2016) and subsequent outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and Equatorial Guinea. While no comparative studies have evaluated the IPC ring approach, field experience suggests it is associated with improved identification and isolation of suspected cases, though challenges in triage remain. Isolation of suspected or confirmed cases is a cornerstone of IPC. Ideally, patients should be isolated in single rooms, with clear separation between suspected and confirmed cases to prevent cross-contamination. Isolation facilities should include dedicated hand hygiene stations, waste bins, sharps containers, and separate areas for donning and doffing PPE. Items and equipment should not be moved between isolation areas to prevent contamination. For example, child-friendly isolation facilities should be designed to promote development and a sense of security.
